articles.title: Twin Bridge targets up to $600M for debut secondaries fund
articles.content: Twin Bridge targets up to $600M for debut secondaries fund Madeline Shi Wed, September 23, 2026 at 1:17 PM EDT 2 min read Twin Bridge Capital Partners , a fund-of-funds manager focused on the small and lower-middle market, is raising its first dedicated private equity secondaries fund. The Chicago firm is looking to raise up to $600 million for the fund, dubbed the Twin Bridge Amplify Fund, according to a person familiar with the matter. The fund held an interim close in December with $300 million from an anchor investor and is expected to reach a final close in the first half of 2027, they added. The Amplify fund will primarily target single-asset continuation fund deals, mainly alongside existing sponsor relationships, the firm said on its website. A quarter of the fund can go towards co-investments, with up to 20% set aside for tactical opportunities arising from market dislocation. Amplify will write checks of around $20 million to $40 million for companies with an average enterprise value of $1 billion or less, according to the person. Twin Bridge declined to comment on the fundraising. The raise puts Twin Bridge among the growing ranks of managers seeking capital to capture booming secondary-market activity. Secondary deal volume reached a record $121 billion in the first half of the year, with over half of this coming in the form of GP-led deals , according to Evercore, the most active intermediary in the market. Single-asset continuation funds totaled about $34 billion in that period, accounting for 53% of total GP-led volume. ICG , Carlyle AlpInvest and Lexington Partners are among the established secondaries investors to have launched funds dedicated to investing in single-asset continuation funds, but their transactions skew to the larger end of the market, according to PitchBook data. Twin Bridge's fund enters a much less crowded part of the market. Comparable firms include NorthSands Capital , founded in 2023 by former Blackstone senior managing director Bruce McEvoy, and Orchard Investment Partners , founded in 2024 by former Madison Dearborn Partners' executives Scott Pasquini and Mark Tresnowski. In addition to the inaugural secondary fund, Twin Bridge is seeking capital for the Twin Bridge Narrow Gate Fund III, its third pool backing small buyout funds, according to a July filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The two funds are the latest in a busy stretch for Twin Bridge, which wrapped up its sixth flagship fund of funds in May, with more than $855 million in capital. articles.title: What Freight Operators Should Actually Be Watching
articles.content: What Freight Operators Should Actually Be Watching FreightWaves Staff Wed, September 23, 2026 at 12:55 PM EDT 4 min read Sean Dehan breaks down Truckstop strategy and the freight market view on FW Today.Truckstop Chief Operating & Strategy Officer Sean Dehan joins FreightWaves to talk through what he's seeing in the market, how strategy is shifting and what matters for freight operators right now. Straight discussion, no filler.#FreightWaves #Truckstop #FreightMarket Spot market load volume on Truckstop's platform is tracking roughly 20% above year-ago levels in September, with flatbed freight posting its strongest year-over-year gains since 2008 — surpassing even the COVID-era surge — according to Sean Dehan, COO and Chief Strategy Officer of Truckstop. Dehan made the remarks in an interview on FreightWaves Today, offering a data-forward read on a market defined by diverging segment performance, persistent cost pressure, and mounting legal uncertainty for brokers. Dehan said spot overflow is the clearest signal of tightening conditions. With roughly two-thirds of September complete at the time of the interview, Truckstop's platform was already up 15% year over year, putting the full-month figure on pace for about 20%. "We're about 15% year over year in September, and we're about two-thirds of the way through September," Dehan said. "So I'd expect us to be somewhere around 20% year over year up on load volume in September." The flatbed segment is the standout, fueled largely by data center construction and broader AI infrastructure investment. Dehan said those drivers have pushed Truckstop's flatbed volumes to levels not seen since 2008, eclipsing the COVID spike. Van and reefer, by contrast, are telling a capacity story more than a demand story. Some shippers facing proposed contract rate increases of 10% to 15% on linehaul box freight are at least exploring intermodal alternatives, though Dehan noted that even if intermodal doubled its share, it would remain a small fraction of the overall truckload market — and drayage capacity is already tight. "Really being ignorant to the data is not going to be a defense in the court of law that you had a reasonable standard of care," Dehan said, explaining why broker customers are now demanding more carrier safety data than ever before. On costs, Dehan said carriers are seeing margin pressure from multiple directions. Insurance premiums have risen 10% to 20% annually for four or five successive years, and diesel prices have reached record levels — including, Dehan noted, a first-ever $10-per-gallon reading in California. Spot carriers have some natural buffer because spot rates adjust faster than contract fuel surcharges, but prolonged fuel increases can still erode margins, particularly on unfamiliar lanes. Story Continues Dehan framed the broader rate environment through an internal Truckstop chart that plots actual dry van linehaul rates against an inflation-adjusted baseline starting around 2005, using a 3% annual inflation assumption. After years of running below that line, rates have only recently climbed back to it. "All we've really done after going way below that average adjusted inflation line is we finally have gotten back to it — we're just barely above it," he said, adding that regulatory and safety-compliance frameworks have effectively re-baselined the market to an inflationary rate floor. The interview also covered the legal fallout from the Montgomery and Lupus decisions affecting freight brokerage liability. Dehan said Montgomery was the "shot over the bow" but the Lupus case — which raised the question of whether a carrier using a C.H. Robinson app could be considered a borrowed employee of the brokerage — was "the actual cannonball that hit the ship." He said larger, compliance-ready brokers view the new environment as a potential competitive advantage, but warned that basic broker practices such as requiring carrier tracking could expose firms to claims of operational control over drivers. Dehan said Truckstop is developing tools to let carriers proactively share their own safety data with brokers, shifting vetting from a one-sided surveillance model to a more collaborative process. Truckstop's platform is tracking roughly 20% above year-ago spot load volumes in September, with flatbed year-over-year gains at their highest since 2008, surpassing even COVID-era peaks. Carrier insurance premiums have risen 10%–20% annually for four to five consecutive years, and diesel hit a record $10 per gallon in California, squeezing margins even as spot rates improve. Post-Montgomery and Lupus rulings, broker customers are demanding more carrier safety data; Truckstop expects carriers to begin proactively sharing internal safety processes to stand out in vetting. articles.title: Diesel Export Ban? Why It Could Backfire Fast
articles.content: Diesel Export Ban? Why It Could Backfire Fast FreightWaves Staff Wed, September 23, 2026 at 12:54 PM EDT 3 min read Diesel prices are swinging hard — and even JPMorgan says it doesn't see a clear resolution. John Kingston breaks down the 25-cent futures move, the export ban talk, and why New England, the Gulf Coast and the West Coast would not feel it the same way.If you run freight, buy fuel or watch margins, this is the takeaway: a diesel export ban may look like relief up front, but the regional fallout could make things worse.#DieselPrices #EnergyMarkets #FreightWaves Talk of a U.S. ban on diesel exports is gaining political traction, but the policy could create sharply uneven outcomes across regions rather than delivering broad price relief — and it would almost certainly trigger refinery run cuts that reduce overall fuel supply, according to FreightWaves energy reporter John Kingston. The export ban discussion comes as diesel futures swung through a 25-cent range in a single session, a move Kingston attributed in part to President Trump's remarks at the United Nations about potentially "annihilating" Iran, the world's fourth or fifth largest oil producer. "Talk of annihilating the world's 4th or 5th largest oil producer is always going to be bullish," Kingston said. "That's just the way it is." The U.S. has not banned the export of any commodity since lifting its crude oil export ban in 2015 following the shale boom. Kingston said the structural problem with a diesel export ban is the country's regional supply imbalance: New England has no nearby refineries and depends heavily on imports from Europe. Banning U.S. exports would tighten European supply, making those imports more expensive or scarce, while the Colonial Pipeline — which moves product from the Gulf Coast to New York Harbor — is likely already running at full capacity and cannot absorb additional volume. "You can imagine some truck drivers sort of reveling in an export ban, because it will flood certain markets with lots of oil, and it'll leave other markets starved," Kingston said. The West Coast faces a similar problem: Gulf Coast diesel cannot reach it easily without transiting the Panama Canal, a lengthy and costly routing. Kingston added that tanker rates are currently "off the charts," further limiting the ability to redirect barrels even with a Jones Act waiver in place. A ban would also remove a key incentive for refiners to keep output high. Refiners have been running at maximum capacity because diesel and gasoline margins are exceptionally profitable. Losing export market access would prompt run cuts, reducing supplies of diesel, gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil simultaneously. Kingston noted that refinery seasonal maintenance is already set to reduce system-wide output, compounding the effect. JP Morgan's commodity research team underscored the broader uncertainty last week, issuing a report that acknowledged it sees no resolution to elevated energy prices — a notable admission from a major Wall Street bank whose analysts had identified $100 Brent crude, a 5-handle on the 10-year Treasury yield, and $4 gasoline as red lines that would prompt a policy shift, none of which proved decisive. Story Continues On the trucking regulatory front, Kingston noted the federal government has issued a first-of-its-kind nationwide hours-of-service waiver for fuel haulers since the COVID-era waiver that ran for more than a year and a half. He also flagged the ongoing Lujan case regarding commercial driver's licenses and upcoming appearances at the Trimble Users Meeting in San Diego and an NMFTA cybersecurity conference in Long Beach, where artificial intelligence's role in freight system security is expected to be a central topic. A U.S. diesel export ban could flood Gulf Coast spot markets while leaving East Coast and West Coast consumers undersupplied due to pipeline and tanker constraints. JP Morgan's commodity research team publicly said last week it sees no resolution to high energy prices, noting that $100 Brent, $4 gasoline, and a 5-handle on the 10-year yield failed to shift administration policy. Refiners running at full capacity to maximize profits would cut production runs if export markets are restricted, reducing supplies of gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil alongside diesel. articles.title: Diesel Prices Could Push More Capacity Out in Q4
articles.content: Diesel Prices Could Push More Capacity Out in Q4 FreightWaves Staff Wed, September 23, 2026 at 12:53 PM EDT 3 min read Diesel prices could push more capacity out in Q4 — and that may be the real freight market story. RXO's Corey Klujsza breaks down why spot demand looks softer, why contract routing guides are shifting, and why carrier costs still leave the market vulnerable to higher rate volatility.This FreightWaves Today segment digs into consumer demand, food and bev seasonality, linehaul pressure and what rising fuel means for truckload capacity heading into peak season. Spot linehaul rates are running more than 40% above year-ago levels, yet the average carrier's operating margin remains far below where it stood at the peak of the last upcycle — a gap that Corey Klujsza, VP of Pricing and Procurement at RXO, says could push more trucks out of the market heading into the fourth quarter. Rising diesel costs are simultaneously squeezing consumers and eroding carrier profitability, setting up a supply-side catalyst even if demand stays muted. Klujsza told FreightWaves that the freight market started Q3 with spot rates "inching towards all-time highs" around the Fourth of July before cooling over the past several weeks. He attributed part of that softening to mini-bid activity that has re-rated contract lanes, pulling volume away from the spot market rather than reflecting a genuine demand collapse. Still, he acknowledged that underlying consumer demand is weakening, driven largely by elevated fuel and food prices. "The linehaul yield for the average carrier in the market is really nowhere close to what it was in the past cycle. Now, all-in transportation spend is inching closer to all-time highs, but really, again, we're contributing and attributing a lot of that to the diesel cost." On the demand side, Klujsza said an apparent uptick in goods consumption is misleading. He argued that much of the recent goods-spending data reflects surging energy costs rather than a true rebound in consumer purchases, cautioning that stripping out fuel leaves the underlying freight demand picture looking softer than headline numbers suggest. He added that Q4 peak season indicators currently point to a muted outcome similar to last year, when freight volumes didn't meaningfully accelerate until just before Thanksgiving. One data point offering a sliver of optimism: the Cass Freight Shipment Index posted its first year-over-year positive print in roughly 40 to 42 months in August, going back to approximately January 2023. Klujsza said the print matters specifically because it measures volume falling to the for-hire market, which could indicate that shippers are being forced outside dedicated and private fleets — a development that would benefit brokers and spot carriers. Story Continues On contract rates, Klujsza said shippers that took on underpriced lanes in Q1 and Q2 are now being forced to reset those rates, narrowing the spot-to-contract premium. He expects full 2027 contract bids to reflect double-digit year-over-year increases, saying "single digits really won't cut it going into 2027, given the timing of the last procurement event." He added that the pace of spot rate acceleration seen from Q2 into Q3 is likely largely behind the market, but inflationary pressure will persist. Shippers are also paring down their carrier and broker networks in response to heightened fraud and compliance risk, Klujsza said. Rather than expanding their routing guide "tail" to chase capacity as they typically would in a tightening market, many shippers are consolidating with partners that meet stricter vetting and compliance standards. "Chasing that compliance and chasing that service just isn't worth it right now," he said, citing the legal exposure created by recent court decisions affecting shipper liability. Spot linehaul rates are up more than 40% year over year, but carrier operating yields remain well below prior-cycle peaks, keeping capacity-exit pressure elevated. The Cass Freight Shipment Index posted its first year-over-year positive print in roughly 40 to 42 months in August, a potential signal of tightening for-hire demand. RXO expects double-digit contract rate increases in Q4 2027 bids, with the current spot-to-contract premium narrowing but spot still trading at a premium. articles.title: Trucking Insurance Fraud: Is Your Fleet Really Covered?
articles.content: Trucking Insurance Fraud: Is Your Fleet Really Covered? FreightWaves Staff Wed, September 23, 2026 at 12:52 PM EDT 3 min read The milk in your fridge has an expiration date, but what about your trucking insurance? Learn how outdated insurance policies create massive liabilities for carriers, brokers, and shippers. Andy Sharpe from MeshVI reveals how real-time, VIN-level data can prevent costly gaps and tackle pervasive insurance fraud in logistics. Don't let stale data put your operation at risk. Up to 15% of certificates of insurance circulating in the trucking industry contain errors or omissions, and insurance costs for motor carriers have tripled or more in the post-Montgomery ruling environment, according to Andy Sharpe, founder and CEO of MeshVI. The company, which launched in 2019, has built an insurance operations platform aimed at giving retail insurance agencies real-time, VIN- and driver-level coverage data — the kind of granular information freight brokers and shippers are now demanding but that most legacy agency management systems were never designed to produce. The problem, Sharpe explained, begins well before a truck hits the road. Traditional certificates of insurance are generated once and reviewed at annual renewal, leaving fleets vulnerable to coverage lapses in between. He described the exposure using a simple analogy: "You've got a best-by date. Well, how do you know the milk didn't spoil yesterday by the time you go to drink it or use it?" A single uncovered vehicle or excluded driver on a cargo claim can force freight brokers or shippers to absorb out-of-pocket costs that a properly maintained policy would have covered. The operational strain on insurance agencies is a critical but underreported bottleneck. One MeshVI customer told Sharpe it receives 1,000 requests per week from insurance monitoring platforms — volume that has surged since the Supreme Court ruling in the Montgomery case pushed those platforms to demand VIN-level and sometimes driver-level data. Without a purpose-built tool, agency staff resort to copying and pasting records manually, compounding error risk. "If the insurance people can't keep track of it, how are the logistics consumers supposed to?" Sharpe said. MeshVI's core product, Mesh Verified, sits inside the insurance agency workflow rather than on the broker or carrier side. Agencies grant downstream access to motor carriers, who can then integrate with electronic logging devices to cross-reference auto liability vehicle schedules, cargo policies for independent contractors, and occupational accident policies against actual operating assets. The platform flags "missing assets" — trucks running in a fleet that are not scheduled on any active policy — a scenario Sharpe said has grown more common over roughly the past five years as non-admitted carriers began writing more restrictive auto liability policies with scheduled-driver requirements and driver exclusions tied to MVR results. Story Continues Certificate fraud compounds the coverage gap problem. Sharpe cited examples of operators insuring a single unit while running 75 trucks, and referenced state-assigned risk insurance plans — including one in Illinois that has drawn fraud reports — where flat pricing applies regardless of fleet size or safety record. "If somebody is going to be in there scheduling one unit, how do you know they're not scheduling those other 74 units in your example? You can't," Sharpe said. MeshVI recently added a fraud-reporting tool to its platform and is working with state programs to reduce their administrative burden while surfacing fraudulent filings. Sharpe, who describes himself as a second-generation truck insurance specialist with more than 25 years in the industry, said he conceived the shared-platform idea in 2012 but found the internet infrastructure insufficient at the time. The company launched in 2019 and has since positioned its verified data feed as a live source that brokers, shippers, and TMS providers can consume directly, bypassing the stale certificate workflow that plaintiff attorneys have increasingly used to establish carrier and broker liability in nuclear verdict cases. Certificates of insurance carry error or omission rates of 5% to 15%, and trucking insurance premiums have risen to three times or more their pre-Montgomery ruling levels. MeshVI's platform gives retail insurance agencies a real-time, VIN- and driver-level data tool to handle surging monitoring requests — one agency reported receiving 1,000 such requests per week. The company is working with state-assigned risk pools to combat fleet insurance fraud, where operators may insure one truck while running dozens more without coverage. articles.title: Brookfield’s GGP scores $800M CMBS refi for Oakbrook Center
articles.content: Brookfield’s GGP scores $800M CMBS refi for Oakbrook Center TRD Staff Wed, September 23, 2026 at 12:30 PM EDT 2 min read BAM GGP CEO Kevin McCrain with 100 Oakbrook Center in Oak Brook (Getty, GGP, LinkedIn, Oakbrook Center) Brookfield Asset Management's retail arm GGP is locking in an $800 million commercial mortgage-backed security refinancing for one of the last large, functioning malls in suburban Chicago. A syndicate comprising Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citibank, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo are reportedly the originators and sellers of the $800 million loan, according to Bisnow. The CMBS loan is set to repay a previous $700 million CMBS loan tied to the Oakbrook Center at 100 Oakbrook Center in the suburb of Oak Brook, as well as pay off $30 million in early payoff penalties. The remainder of the cash will go to closing costs at $5 million and return $65 million of equity to the sponsors, according to the outlet. The loan has a five-year interest-only term, and has an assumed rate of 5.9 percent. In July 2026, the mall was 94 percent leased with around 160 unique tenants, according to the outlet. Oakbrook Center is the second-largest shopping mall in the Chicago metro and not only came out of the pandemic alive, but thriving. In 2020, previous reporting from The Real Deal noted that the 2.6 million-square-foot mall was 82 percent leased. Macy's, Nordstrom and Neiman Marcus anchored the mall during the height of the pandemic. Also in 2020, Morgan Stanley provided the property with another $475 million refinancing package. Securing refinancing proved a success compared to other mall owners across the nation who were kicking the keys back to lenders, due to a sharp decline in foot traffic and a pandemic-era rise in e-commerce. Oakbrook Center is noted for its luxury stores, meant to attract affluent shoppers from the wealthy Oak Brook suburb. In 2025, LANA, a fine jeweler, moved its flagship location in downtown Winnetka to the Oakbrook Center. In 2024, Google selected the shopping mall for its first Midwest retail storefront, a 3,500-square-foot brick-and-mortar location that was only the tech giant's fifth of its kind at the time. — Hunter Cooke Read more Fine jeweler LANA moving flagship to Brookfield's Oakbrook Center Brookfield lands $475M refi on Oakbrook Center Here's what tenants are paying at Brookfield's Oakbrook Center mall This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. articles.title: Renishaw Rides the AI Chip Boom to Record Results
articles.content: Renishaw Rides the AI Chip Boom to Record Results Mark Nichols Wed, September 23, 2026 at 12:18 PM EDT 4 min read NVDA RSW.L Renishaw Rides the AI Chip Boom to Record Results - Moby THE GIST Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here. Renishaw has landed in one of the more profitable corners of the AI investment boom, supplying the ultra-precise measurement technology needed to manufacture increasingly complicated semiconductors. Record sales, stronger margins and a growing order book pushed full-year results ahead of expectations, while management says the new financial year has started strongly as chip-equipment demand continues to accelerate. WHAT HAPPENED Renishaw shares rose around 3% after the Gloucestershire-based engineering group reported record results for the year to June and said it expects further strong progress in revenue, profit and operating margin. Revenue increased 14% to £815.8 million (about $1.1 billion) and rose 17% at constant currencies, slightly ahead of the roughly £810 million analysts had expected. Adjusted operating profit climbed 36% to £152.9 million, lifting the margin to 18.7% from 15.7%, while adjusted pretax profit rose 32% to a record £168 million, beating consensus of about £165 million. Adjusted earnings per share increased 30% to 179.5p, also slightly ahead of expectations, while statutory pretax profit rose 27% to £150 million despite £18 million of redundancy and other one-off costs. Momentum accelerated as the year progressed. Fourth-quarter revenue reached a record £244.2 million, up 28% year on year, while the order book continued to grow. Position Measurement was the standout division, with revenue jumping 26% to £260.9 million and adjusted operating profit increasing 53% to £71.5 million. Its margin expanded to 27.4% from 22.5%, driven largely by demand for optical encoders used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Specialised Technologies grew even faster, with revenue up 43% to £107.5 million as additive-manufacturing systems benefited from aerospace and defense demand. The division swung from a £9.9 million adjusted operating loss to a £4.7 million profit. Industrial Metrology, still the largest part of the group, grew more slowly at 4% as weakness in some traditional industrial markets offset demand for newer metrology systems and software. The balance sheet remained strong, with cash and deposits rising to £291 million. Renishaw increased its regular dividend by 5% to 82p per share and added a special 70p interim dividend. WHY IT MATTERS Renishaw's results show how far the AI boom reaches beyond the companies designing chips or building data centers. Story Continues One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here. Semiconductor factories rely on machines capable of positioning components with extraordinary accuracy, and Renishaw's encoders measure movement and position throughout that manufacturing process. As chip designs become more complex and production tolerances shrink, precision becomes increasingly valuable. That creates a useful combination of cyclical and structural growth. Semiconductor equipment demand naturally moves through cycles, but the current investment wave is being amplified by the enormous processing requirements of artificial intelligence. Renishaw says demand from semiconductor and electronics manufacturing equipment builders has reached unprecedented levels, particularly across Asia. APAC revenue rose 17% at constant currencies to £381.9 million, largely because of encoder demand from those customers. The Americas grew even faster at 35%, helped by high-value capital equipment sales into aerospace, defense and power generation, while EMEA increased a more modest 3%. The margin performance matters almost as much as the revenue growth. Renishaw delivered roughly £20 million of cost savings during the year, while higher volumes allowed revenue to grow considerably faster than engineering, distribution and administrative expenses. That operating leverage pushed the adjusted margin three percentage points higher even after currency headwinds, while the second-half margin moved above 20%. There are still reasons not to assume every year will look this good. Management itself acknowledges that semiconductor markets move through multiyear cycles, while competition is increasing in China as local rivals offer cheaper products that are good enough for less demanding applications. Cash conversion also slipped to 79% from 91% as the company invested more working capital to support record sales and a larger order book. The key question is therefore how much of today's semiconductor strength becomes lasting market-share growth before the cycle eventually turns. WHAT'S NEXT The early signs for FY27 remain encouraging, with management saying the year has started strongly and that semiconductor manufacturing equipment continues to drive demand. Investors will watch whether Position Measurement can maintain its exceptional growth and whether Specialised Technologies can build on its return to profitability as aerospace, defense and additive manufacturing expand. Renishaw is also getting closer to its medium-term ambition of operating margins above 20%, which would make future revenue growth considerably more valuable if management can sustain the cost discipline delivered this year. For now, the company has turned the AI spending boom into something unusually tangible: more encoders, record revenue and a much fatter profit margin. articles.title: Trump and Xi begin high-stakes summit in Washington
articles.content: US President Donald Trump, right, greets Xi Jinping after the Chinese president’s plane landed at a military base near Washington last night © Getty Images Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on x (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on facebook (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on linkedin (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on x (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on facebook (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on linkedin (opens in a new window) Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extend trade truce to January on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Myles McCormick in Washington Published September 24 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected] Hello from Washington and welcome to White House Watch. On our agenda today: Trump and Xi meet in Washington for pivotal summit Influencer Hasan Piker says Republican efforts to vilify him are falling short Republicans are splashing out on midterm election advertising All eyes are on Washington today, where Xi Jinping has arrived for a high-stakes two-day summit with Donald Trump (Follow along with the FT’s live blog here ). It is the Chinese president’s first visit to the US capital in more than a decade. And as my colleagues Demetri Sevastopulo and Joe Leahy report , it will involve plenty of fanfare. At the top of the agenda are trade relations and the creation of an AI dialogue to discuss risks posed by the technology. Shortly after Xi landed last night, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the countries had agreed to extend their one-year trade truce, which was set to expire on November 10, until January 10. Xi is also expected to raise the subject of Taiwan. Trump sparked alarm in May when he said American arms sales to Taiwan were a “good negotiating chip” , suggesting that he might curtail US support for Taipei. But there will also be plenty of pomp and cultural events. A formal welcome ceremony will be held on the South Lawn of the White House this morning, featuring a military review and flyover by fighter jets and bombers. Trump and Xi walk side by side during the arrival ceremony. The Chinese president later said the two countries should be ‘partners, not rivals’ © Getty Images In the evening, the pair will be joined by their wives and a host of Big Tech and Wall Street executives for an official state dinner. On the guest list are Tesla boss Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, Jane Fraser from Citigroup and Apple’s former chief Tim Cook. In a statement issued after his arrival last night, Xi said it was a “great pleasure” to pay a state visit to the US. The two countries should be “partners, not rivals”, the Chinese leader said, adding that 2026 was a “pivotal” year for US-China relations. Trump’s show of respect for his Chinese counterpart underlines the shift from his aggressive stance towards Beijing during his first term — an approach that has frustrated the ambitions of the hawks in his administration . But the US president’s changeable nature and willingness to deploy tariffs as a geopolitical weapon mean nothing is certain in the relationship. Amid all the fanfare of the next two days, the world will be watching attentively. Could you be the FT’s next stock picking champion? The FT’s new Stock Picking Game is a fast, fun way to test your trading instincts, sharpen your market expertise and compete for the chance to win £1,000. Terms and conditions apply. Register for season two now. The latest headlines Republicans are far outspending Democrats on advertising ahead of November 3’s midterm elections, reserving roughly $1bn in advertising slots between September 1 and election day, according to an FT analysis. A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to temporarily restore White House access to CNN, MS Now and Politico after the news outlets had been banned by the president. A global bond rout has deepened as oil jumped back above $105 a barrel on Thursday, adding to inflation fears after the US Treasury market suffered its biggest fall since last year’s trade war sell-off. The US oil industry also warned there was no “silver bullet” solution to the supply crunch. Belgium’s foreign ministry has warned internally that the US under Trump is no longer a reliable ally , according to a document seen by the FT. The UK is reviewing its plan to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, after Trump renewed his opposition to the deal in a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham. What we’re hearing Leftwing influencer Hasan Piker was accused by House Speaker Mike Johnson this month of wanting to lead the US down a “dark, dangerous, deadly road to communism”. But the prolific Twitch streamer — seen by many on the right as one of the most dangerous men in the country — told my colleague Guy Chazan that Republicans’ campaign of vilification “isn’t working”. “If you talk to me you very quickly realise I’m a fairly pragmatic person,” he told the FT, adding that the Financial Times was his “favourite newspaper”. Hasan Piker speaks at a Democratic campaign event in Michigan in April © Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Piker is a self-declared “socialist anti-imperialist” who once said America “deserved 9/11” (for which he later apologised) and has enraged supporters of Israel by saying that he would “vote for Hamas over Israel every time”. He was also banned in June from entering the UK because his presence “may not be conducive to the public good”. In an interview with the FT, the bogeyman of the Republican Party hit back at attempts to brand him a “dangerous, radical, Islamist, jihadist terrorist”. “A lot of these manosphere guys don’t know what they’re talking about — their level of involvement with politics is super, super basic,” Piker said. Viewpoints Donald Trump’s proposed diesel export ban will backfire , according to Lex’s Camilla Palladino. Martin Wolf says the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates in spite of Trump’s demands was “sensible” and “overdue” . Calling for closer EU-Canada ties without pooling sovereignty is an abdication of European responsibility , argues Martin Sandbu. As Germany’s Friedrich Merz comes under pressure and speculation grows over who could succeed him at the helm of Europe’s biggest economy, Janan Ganesh maintains the west does not have a leadership problem . While existential fears over technology rise, the FT editorial board says the US and China can work together on AI security . articles.title: Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth
articles.content: Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on x (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on facebook (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on linkedin (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on x (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on facebook (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on linkedin (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Helen Bain . Photography by Wendy Huynh Published September 25 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. At the age of 29, Jacques Testard set up a publishing house because no one in publishing would employ him. Born in France and schooled in London, he had wanted to go into academia before a series of internships made him realise that publishing was “another way to be serious about books”. In 2014, when he struggled to find a permanent opening, he decided to launch his own house. His ambition was not just to be an editor but to find and publish “writers at the cutting edge of contemporary literature” – including, significantly, work in translation. He had 18 months until the money ran out. “I thought, ‘I’ll give this a go and see what happens, and maybe in a few years’ time someone will give me a job.’” Every publisher is a story, says Ray O’Meara, the house’s art director, and the story of Fitzcarraldo Editions is very simple. Twelve years ago, mainstream UK publishers did not believe there was a market for translated literature. It was a gap Testard was able to plug. The first book he published that year was Zone by Mathias Énard, a 521-page stream-of-consciousness account of an amphetamine-fuelled journey across Italy, written in a single sentence, which he had discovered when he read it in French. For the new house, it was something of a mission statement. That same year, still the sole employee, Testard made an offer for Svetlana Alexievich’s oral history Second-hand Time . The book was already a bestseller in Russia and had sold well in France and Germany but there was no competition for the UK rights. Testard’s opening bid of $2,000 was rejected; he upped it a little and it was accepted. The following year Alexievich won the Nobel Prize in Literature and there was an eight-way auction for the US rights. The publisher aims to select works that are “innovative, imaginative, ambitious” © Wendy Huynh Today, Fitzcarraldo Editions has become a hallmark for a generation. Its signature International Klein Blue and clean cream titles include Nobel- and Pulitzer-prize winners, with authors ranging from French memoirist Annie Ernaux to New York-based war reporter Jon Lee Anderson and Hong Kong novelist Dorothy Tse. It specialises in contemporary literary fiction and long-form essays, seeking out work that is determinedly “innovative, imaginative, ambitious”, broadly kept at a 50-50 split between English language and literature in translation. Cult hits include Perfection by Vincenzo Latronico , an interrogation of millennial life; The Plague , essays on death and humanity by PEN Pinter-award-winner Jacqueline Rose; and this year’s Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life: Voices From Gaza by Samar Yazbek. A poetry list launched last year: this May, American poet Sasha Debevec-McKenney won the Dylan Thomas Prize for her debut collection Joy Is My Middle Name , while Makenna Goodman’s novel Helen of Nowhere is currently longlisted for the Booker Prize. It’s an extraordinary outcome for a house that started out with a single employee, 18 months’ funding, and the modest aim of publishing six books a year. “I feel fortunate to have started a press when I did,” says Testard with understatement when we meet in Fitzcarraldo’s offices in a former factory in Peckham Rye, south-east London. “I guess I turned up at the right time.” Fitzcarraldo founder and publisher Jacques Testard © Wendy Huynh “Fitzcarraldo is forging ahead on its own path and terms,” says Harriet Moore, literary agent at Alexander Aitken. “They have a robust commitment to the long view, a confidence in their own sensibility and vision, and their books will last. It offers a place where writers can think seriously and strangely, work against the expected, follow their obsessions, play.” “Jacques is concerned about quality, not quantity,” says Norwegian writer Jon Fosse , who won the Nobel Prize in 2023; Fitzcarraldo had published Septology , a seven-part novel in a single sentence, the previous year. “He has trusted me.” Fosse had won numerous international awards, but his prose was not published in the UK until Fitzcarraldo released Scenes from a Childhood in 2018. “Jacques is an attentive editor who gives excellent advice and is deeply respectful of authors,” says Ernaux. The Years had been published to acclaim in France in 2008 but it was not until 2018 that Fitzcarraldo published the translation to a rapturous reception, credited as contributing towards Ernaux’s 2022 Nobel win. (Testard had argued the case to nominate it for the International Booker despite it being hybrid-memoir rather than fiction; it was shortlisted.) It now seems absurd that Ernaux, Fosse and Alexievich (as well as Nobel-winner Olga Tokarczuk , whose Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead is a Fitzcarraldo bestseller) had not been published in the UK sooner. Testard shrugs when this is put to him, pointing out that when Fitzcarraldo launched there was still a tendency in bookshops to shelve international literature in its own category, “almost labelling it as a separate genre”. He attributes this partly to a British Empire legacy; that with the Commonwealth there’s “a sense that you’re [already] bringing writers in from the peripheries”. There is also the commercial aspect – “this notion that translation is more expensive, and you’ll never be able to recoup the money”. But there is also the question of discovering it in the first place. Testard grew up reading “indiscriminately” in English and French, and he also reads Spanish. “There are very, very few editors in UK publishing who read in other languages,” he says. “In Spain or France or Germany you have to have three or four languages to be in the editorial positions we are in.” At the Fitzcarraldo Editions office in Peckham, south London. From left: operations executive Samir Chadha, associate publisher Tamara Sampey-Jawad, operations director Jennifer Tighe, editor Charlotte Jackson and editor and publicist Emma Berrill © Wendy Huynh Testard, 41, possesses the extreme courtesy often typical of his generation, underscored by a certain steel. Wearing a collarless blue shirt and dark trousers, he talks fluently and rapidly about how his frustrations with the anglophone publishing industry brought him where he is today. The open-plan space, now housing 11 employees, is all white walls and deep-blue accents, light pouring in from the Crittall-style windows. On an exposed brick wall at one end of the room, trademark blue-and-white spines are lined up in rows, while in the small, bare meeting room, coloured Post-Its stuck on a wall denote the year’s publishing schedule: non-fiction, fiction, poetry, classics. Outside, over the railway line, sits Peckham Levels, the multistorey car park turned cultural hub where Fitzcarraldo holds its annual party each summer. Testard’s gravitas echoes across the house – although sometimes this effect seems almost accidental. “Can we do that?”, O’Meara recalls wondering when Testard first suggested taking the name Fitzcarraldo from Werner Herzog’s 1982 film about an opera-loving fanatic rampaging around the Peruvian jungle. Your browser does not support playing this file but you can still download the MP3 file to play locally. Labour officials in Downing Street and beyond have discussed the parameters in which a snap election could be called. Will Andy Burnham take the gamble? As speculation about the idea grips Westminster, host Lucy Fisher is joined by political editor George Parker and deputy political editor Jim Pickard to weigh up the risks and rewards of going to the public early. They also look ahead to the Labour Party conference in Liverpool starting this weekend, and the troubles that lie ahead for UK-EU relations. Plus George reports back from Burnham’s first major international summit at the UN general assembly in New York, where the prime minister weathered his first encounter with Donald Trump. Follow Lucy on X or Bluesky @LOS_Fisher , @lucyfisher.ft.com ; George on @georgewparker.bsky.social , @GeorgeWParker ; Jim @PickardJE Want more? The risks of calling an early election for Andy Burnham Treasury open to smaller fiscal headroom to reduce UK tax rises The FT’s budget dashboard: the data confronting chancellor John Healey Labour conference set to vote on new AI regulator as cabinet concerns grow Donald Trump rejects ‘globalist scheme’ to control AI in blow to Andy Burnham UK to provide military support to Saudi Arabia in its fight with Houthi rebels How could John Healey raise tax in the budget Sign up here f or Stephen Bush's morning newsletter Inside Politics for straight-talking insight into the stories that matter, plus puns and tongue (mostly) in cheek. articles.title: In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait
articles.content: In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on x (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on facebook (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on linkedin (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on whatsapp (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on x (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on facebook (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on linkedin (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Maria Shollenbarger . Photography by Ramona Balaban Published September 26 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. “I never really designed this space,” says 30-year-old artist and designer Paolo del Gallo di Roccagiovine. “It simply grew around my work.” We’re in an early-18th-century palazzo midway down the ruler-straight stretch of Rome’s Via del Babuino , three floors above the street’s neat ranks of artisan and designer boutiques. The grand, high-ceilinged apartment that del Gallo has welcomed me into has been owned by his family for generations; today its warren of rooms has been conscripted for his various artistic projects. A bed designed by del Gallo using a baroque headboard from the family collection © Ramona Balaban “Its last permutation was as my grandfather’s law office,” del Gallo continues. “At some point he emptied it completely, intending to figure out what to do with it at a later date.” Then Covid came. “My brother, my two sisters and I moved in very quickly to distance ourselves from our parents and grandparents.” Mattresses were thrown onto floors; in place of several of the doors, which had been sent out for restoration, del Gallo hung textiles he’d brought back from India and Uzbekistan. His siblings, he recalls, “arrived with large suitcases full of clothes. I apparently decided that my essentials for surviving lockdown were an antique gilt grotto table, a pair of beautiful chairs and some silver cutlery.” The 18th-century desk that he uses as his work table, covered in studies, drawings and raw materials © Ramona Balaban By 2022, he realised the apartment “had quietly filled itself with my things: paintings, materials, objects I’d collected”. So he came to an arrangement with his family to use it as his atelier – a place to work, receive clients and spend the occasional night in town. Del Gallo’s creative output moves between sculpture, painting, installation and interior-design intervention. Historical objects – a chair, a mirror, a book, a fragment of an ancient Ionic column capital – are “active structures” within his work. An antique hourglass is embellished with a hyperrealist rendering of an exotic butterfly; a pair of 18th-century doors are gilded in patterns like shards of light. An artwork from Paolo del Gallo’s 2025 show Butterfly Effect, along with ceramic sculptures, including one of his ancestor Zénaïde Bonaparte © Ramona Balaban His commissions range from tiny installation-like sculptures of shells and corals to entire ballrooms frescoed to residents’ specifications. Del Gallo’s work can be found across Rome: there’s a large mural inside Villa Europa, the official headquarters of the EU delegation, restoration work at the Belgian Embassy to the Quirinal and the former Belgian Embassy to the Holy See (the Belgian ambassador, Pierre-Emmanuel De Bauw, also owns his work) and pieces in private homes. At his mother’s mid-18th-century villa , the walls are covered in his dreamily atmospheric murals. Del Gallo with one of his artworks in the archive room © Ramona Balaban “What drew me to Paolo’s work was his sensitivity to nature and texture, coupled with his deep love for and integration of his own history,” says New York-based collector Tracey Hejailan-Amon. “What’s striking is how seamlessly these two registers coexist in his practice, and how easily they integrate with other artists’ works.” “Architecture is never simply a backdrop,” says del Gallo, tall and rangy, dressed in an old white button-down shirt with sleeves rolled up and loose trousers. He’s drawn to “spaces that already carry a strong sense of memory. When I work on historical surfaces, like mercury or mirror, it creates a trace that I couldn’t invent myself. I think of it as a kind of collaboration with time.” From left: a neoclassical marble oil lamp – one of his favourite pieces – painted doors he created for a 2021 exhibition at Palazzo Colonna, an oil on raw linen painting of an emu he painted while in Mexico and a door from Palazzo Sacchetti © Ramona Balaban An oil painting on an antique mirror – a work in progress © Ramona Balaban Time and history play an outsized part in del Gallo’s art. His family tree includes Napoleon Bonaparte and the Spanish royal family; he has lived most of his life in grand historic residences. His brothers and sisters pursued more conventional careers while he studied at Rome’s Accademia di Belle Arti. “I don’t remember ever deciding to be an artist,” he says. “I just grew up surrounded by art, and architecture.” At 16, he began practising restoration, which informed his later style; the natural-history books of his ancestor, ornithologist Charles-Lucien Bonaparte, “taught me very early to look closely at nature – its beauty, fragility and complexity”. He brought it permanently into his visual language. The main salon at  del Gallo’s family apartment in Rome has the original palazzo flooring and frescoes on the ceiling. He painted the mural on the walls using natural pigments such as lapis lazuli and Armenian earth © Ramona Balaban In the apartment’s main salon, “the principal theme is day and night”. A combination of stripping back layers of older paint and layering on new ones has resulted in vast semi-abstract murals of cloud and sky. On one wall, a cool white sun projects slightly from the surface; opposite, a pale moon is discernible through darker tones. Del Gallo’s delicate colours – rendered with rare materials such as lapis lazuli dust and Armenian soil – reprise the tones of the original ceiling frescoes. Two canvases, one hung midway up the wall and another leaning next to the fireplace (both unframed, as is del Gallo’s preference), echo the celestial theme at a more contained scale. The 18th-century chest of drawers in the bedroom is a Neapolitan piece. On top is a gilt crucifix from the private chapel of his family’s palace, a carved-bone pyramid and a vase he found in Mexico. He restored and painted the historic walls himself © Ramona Balaban Del Gallo’s penchant for the palimpsest has even reshaped the structure of his surroundings. “Sometimes I wake up convinced that there must be something hidden above a false ceiling, and decide to open it up. One day I imagined there was a fireplace behind a wall; I started drilling, and actually found it there, blocked up, with traces of soot inside.” Del Gallo crafted a new surround, mixing cement, lime and marble dust to create an unadorned frame that’s an elegant counterpoint to the ornate room. “I don’t only work in any one room,” says del Gallo. “It’s difficult to call a single space ‘my studio’ because in reality I make use of the whole apartment. It has become part of the creative process. Inevitably, it influences everything I do.” A corner room full of easels and tables “has the best light, and is where I store most of my materials”. A small but perfectly formed dining room, its walls hung with family porcelain, has a Carlo Scarpa table, covered in the same linen he uses for painting, at which he sometimes alights. The whole space is a locus for artistic experimentation that’s also as intimate and revealing a self-portrait as a home can be. articles.title: A warning of ‘breakdowns and deficiencies’ in security at the US central bank
articles.content: The Fed’s Office of Inspector General warned of potential security breaches at the US central bank © Reuters Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on x (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on x (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Abigail Hauslohner in Washington Published September 29 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected] Hello from Washington and welcome to White House Watch. Here’s what we’re looking at today: Federal Reserve’s watchdog warns of security “deficiencies” at central bank Marco Rubio blames a “foreign actor” for the UK terror plot over the weekend US completes withdrawal of troops from Iraq The Federal Reserve’s watchdog has warned of “breakdowns and deficiencies” in security at the US central bank after a departing official was suspected of removing sensitive information, highlighting vulnerabilities at the institution. The Fed’s Office of Inspector General flagged potential breaches by an unnamed employee in the international finance division, culminating in 279 “data loss prevention” alerts in the 90 days before they retired in July 2024, 111 of these potentially involved information relating to the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee and 40 potentially contained central bank material. “This potential incident highlighted information security risks and control breakdowns and deficiencies that we believe require the board’s immediate attention,” the watchdog wrote in a report released on Monday. Government officials have long harboured concerns about the security of the Fed, which is seen as a high-value target for foreign adversaries because of the board’s proprietary financial information. The watchdog recommended tighter security procedures, which the Fed agreed to implement, but it said there was insufficient basis to pursue a misconduct investigation into the matter. What’s next for the global economy? Economics leader writer Tej Parikh and European economics commentator Martin Sandbu will be answering questions on the next stage of growth, its biggest risks and how global businesses and households will be affected. Submit your question here for the latest instalment of Ask an Expert happening on Thursday October 1. The latest headlines US secretary of state Marco Rubio said a “foreign actor” was involved in a suspected terrorist plot near a British air force base this weekend, in remarks that will intensify global scrutiny of the incident . The US Treasury on Monday took its first concrete steps towards cracking down on a suite of strategies used by wealthy US investors to cut their tax bills . Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece has caused a political stir in Romania after suggesting the US could bring down governments. Trump asked Xi Jinping if China wanted to buy American weapons , US envoy says. Private equity has become an important target on the campaign trail for the US midterms as candidates blame large investors for soaring housing costs . Divisions within Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again movement risk damaging Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. What we’re hearing Happening under the radar this week: the US is completing the withdrawal of most of its forces from Iraq. You would be forgiven for thinking: ‘Didn’t this already happen?’ Yes, it did, in 2011. US forces returned to fight the Islamic State a few years later. And now, 23 years after the initial US invasion of Iraq, nearly all US troops are expected to withdraw from the country by tomorrow. Kurdish leaders in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region of Iraq’s north are unhappy. Masrour Barzani tells my colleague Mehul Srivastava that the Americans are leaving their Kurdish allies without any missile defences and vulnerable to Iranian attack amid a war started by Donald Trump six months ago. “The threat is real,” Barzani said in a recent interview. The abandonment by Washington is “shameful”. Could you be the FT’s next stock picking champion? The FT’s new Stock Picking Game is a fast, fun way to test your trading instincts, sharpen your market expertise and compete for the chance to win £1,000. Terms and conditions apply. Register for season two now. Viewpoints Democrats are likely to make gains in Congress in November’s midterm elections but a divided government is unlikely to derail Trump’s agenda , argues Edward Luce. Jonathan Derbyshire says that, although Republicans are outspending the Democrats by around $1bn to $750mn, they are heading for a historic defeat. For once, the Fed has put Main Street before Wall Street, writes Sheila Bair US accounting editor Stephen Foley highlights how requirements under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act are being rolled back. Your browser does not support playing this file but you can still download the MP3 file to play locally. Recorded in front of an audience at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, host Lucy Fisher and political editor George Parker unpack Andy Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. From rethinking Britain’s relationship with the EU to ending the pensions triple lock and scrapping the electoral system, Burnham laid out an ambitious agenda for the country. Lucy and George speak to business secretary Jonathan Reynolds about the prime minister’s plans, before northern correspondent Jennifer Williams and Inside Politics writer and columnist Stephen Bush join them to give their takeaways from the week. Want more? Free links: Andy Burnham sets up battle lines on social care and Europe How would Andy Burnham’s social care shake-up work? articles.title: Ennis (EBF) Grows Sales but Earns Less. Are Legal Items Hiding a Better Business?
articles.content: Ennis (EBF) Grows Sales but Earns Less. Are Legal Items Hiding a Better Business? Jeff Lewis September 22, 2026 3 min read EBF Ennis, Inc. (NYSE: EBF ) reported higher sales and lower earnings for the quarter ended August 31, 2026, but legal items complicate the comparison. The underlying business held up better than the headline profit decline suggests, while paper costs created genuine margin pressure. The September 21 release showed revenue of $102 million, up 3.3% from $98.7 million. Net earnings fell to $9.4 million from $13.2 million. Investors need to distinguish the litigation effects from changes in demand, acquisition contributions, and production costs. Bull Case The prior-year quarter included a $5.3 million favorable litigation judgment, while the current quarter included an unrelated $700,000 litigation charge. Management said diluted earnings per share increased $0.02 after excluding these items from both periods. This non-GAAP comparison removes the specified litigation effects from reported diluted earnings per share. That modest improvement is more encouraging than the reported earnings decline. Gross profit also increased to $30.5 million from $30.1 million, showing that the larger revenue base produced additional gross profit despite a lower margin. Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) generated $34.1 million of operating cash flow in the first half, compared with $18.4 million a year earlier. Cash reached $54 million as of August 31, and management reported no debt. That financial position provides room to support operations and acquisitions without immediate refinancing pressure. Supply continuity is another positive. Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) has received shipments from alternative carbonless-paper suppliers following the closure of the sole domestic producer. Management continues to expect uninterrupted product availability and customer service. Maintaining supply protects the ability to fulfill orders while the business adapts to higher input costs. Bear Case Acquisitions contributed approximately $2.3 million of the $3.3 million quarterly revenue increase. Subtracting the disclosed acquisition contribution leaves roughly $1 million of additional sales, or about 1% of prior-year revenue, based on rounded figures. The reported growth rate therefore overstates the improvement outside those acquisition contributions. Gross margin declined to 29.9% from 30.5%, a decrease of 60 basis points. Management attributed the decline primarily to higher carbonless-paper costs recognized in cost of sales. That pressure affects the economics of producing and selling printed products independently of the litigation comparison. Story Continues Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) needs pricing, product mix, or productivity improvements to offset those costs. Reliable access to paper addresses availability, while purchasing terms and selling prices determine how much profit remains on each order. Cash generation also requires context. Inventory declined during the quarter after the earlier buildup to protect supply. Investors should assess whether operating cash flow remains strong once inventory levels stabilize, since working-capital movements can change cash generation without equivalent changes in earnings. Hedge Fund Sentiment The filings available so far reflect positions held before Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) reported its quarterly results. Insider Monkey's database showed 15 hedge funds holding Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) at the end of 2Q2026, up from 14 funds three months earlier. Conclusion Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) looks more resilient after accounting for the litigation items, supported by strong first-half cash generation and a debt-free balance sheet. However, acquisition contributions explain most of the quarterly sales increase, and paper costs are squeezing margins. Growth outside acquisitions, gross-margin stabilization, and cash flow after inventory normalization will determine whether the business is improving sustainably. While we acknowledge the potential of EBF as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. articles.title: Strive CEO: Bitcoin Could ‘Go to Infinity' as Dollar Debt Crisis Breaks
articles.content: Strive CEO: Bitcoin Could ‘Go to Infinity' as Dollar Debt Crisis Breaks Darryn Pollock September 22, 2026 2 min read BTC-USD ASST DX-Y.NYB Strive CEO Matt Cole says Bitcoin (BTC) could effectively go to infinity against the US dollar, arguing that a mounting Washington debt crisis, not Bitcoin's own scarcity, is what will ultimately break the currency's value. Cole made the comments on Bloomberg Crypto, as digital assets have reclaimed $3 trillion in market value since January. Strive, a Bitcoin treasury company that raises capital to buy and hold BTC on its balance sheet, has been one of the more aggressive buyers through the cycle. A Debt Crisis, Not a Bitcoin Story Cole argued that the 10-year Treasury yield would already sit north of 10% if the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department stepped back from the bond market entirely. He credits Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent with capping long-end rates for now, but says that intervention only delays a reckoning, since neither party in Washington shows any willingness to cut spending. "We think Bitcoin can effectively go to infinity versus the dollar." — Matt Cole, on Bloomberg https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NFQVh9AH0lM That logic underpins Strive's public forecast of a 50% compound annual growth rate for Bitcoin through 2030, a figure Cole calls conservative given the asset's past bull-market cycles, a view he first laid out when he called the bear market over last month. It also explains why Strive's SATA preferred stock, which pays a daily cash dividend, has, according to Cole, outperformed Bitcoin itself by more than 100% in 2026 even as BTC has traded roughly flat. Why the Treasury Model Persists Cole also pushed back on the idea that the Bitcoin treasury company model is fading. He argues it never broke, only that firms without a clear thesis or sound debt terms struggled once the bear market hit, while disciplined buyers kept accumulating even as Wall Street treasuries resumed buying. Cole's framing puts Bitcoin's price action second to a wager on US fiscal dysfunction, one that only pays off if bond markets and the dollar move the way he expects over the next several years. articles.title: Westinghouse Air Brake (WAB) Signs $700 Million-Plus Rail Services Deal. Can Profits Grow?
articles.content: Westinghouse Air Brake (WAB) Signs $700 Million-Plus Rail Services Deal. Can Profits Grow? Jeff Lewis September 22, 2026 3 min read WAB Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (NYSE: WAB ) announced on September 21 a services agreement worth more than $700 million with La Compagnie du TransGuinéen. Combined with locomotive orders placed in 2024, announced agreements for the Simandou project now exceed $1.2 billion. The railway stretches more than 600 kilometers between the Simandou mine and Guinea's Port of Morebaya. The new agreement extends the relationship beyond locomotive delivery into ongoing fleet support. For investors, the opportunity is to earn revenue throughout the equipment's operating life. Is Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (WAB) The Best Railroad Stock To Buy Now? BULL CASE Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (NYSE:WAB) will provide scheduled and unscheduled maintenance, parts, component overhauls, logistics support, remote diagnostics, and training. These activities create multiple opportunities to serve the same fleet after the initial equipment sale. That is an attractive business model when maintenance needs translate into repeat orders and efficient service delivery. Familiarity with the locomotives should help technicians diagnose problems and plan repairs. Remote monitoring could also help identify faults before they cause prolonged downtime, strengthening the customer's incentive to maintain the relationship. Local workforce development and partnerships with Guinean businesses could improve responsiveness as the operation matures. Over time, an experienced local team could reduce dependence on specialists traveling to the site and make parts planning more efficient. The broader freight business provides a profitable base. Second-quarter freight revenue increased 16.9% to $2.24 billion, while its GAAP operating margin rose to 22.5% from 21.6%. Those results demonstrate existing earnings capacity, although the new agreement's contribution will depend on its own pricing and execution costs. BEAR CASE Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (NYSE:WAB) has announced a multiyear contract value, not $700 million of annual revenue or immediate cash receipts. The combined $1.2 billion also includes earlier equipment orders. Treating the entire amount as new business from this announcement would overstate the incremental opportunity. The release does not specify the exact contract duration, revenue commencement date, annual revenue schedule, or expected service margin. Those details matter because the same headline value can produce very different returns depending on how quickly work is performed, costs are incurred, and customers pay. Story Continues Recurring service opportunities also do not guarantee smooth quarterly growth. Second-quarter freight-services sales declined 4.2%, reflecting lower modernization deliveries, as expected. Maintenance and locomotive rebuilding have different schedules, and the broader services category can still fluctuate. Execution in Guinea will require reliable parts availability, logistics, and trained personnel. If staffing, inventory or transport costs run ahead of expectations, revenue growth could come with disappointing margins. Building local capabilities may also require spending before the full benefits emerge. Cash collection is another test. If parts inventories and customer receivables grow faster than payments arrive, accounting profit could exceed the cash generated by the agreement. Hedge Fund Sentiment The filings available so far reflect positions held before Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (NYSE:WAB) reported its Simandou services agreement. Insider Monkey's database showed 67 hedge funds holding Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (NYSE:WAB) at the end of 2Q2026, up from 63 funds three months earlier. CONCLUSION Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation (NYSE:WAB) has secured a credible extension of locomotive sales into recurring fleet support. The strategic benefit is a longer customer relationship with opportunities to earn beyond equipment delivery. Revenue commencement, service margins, and cash collection will determine the financial payoff. Consistent operating performance and disciplined control of delivery costs are the tests for turning a large contract into durable shareholder value. That ownership calculation excludes the buyer's existing 4.95% stake in Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN:VGZ), which it intends to cancel at completion. For shareholders, the trade-off is a smaller interest in a larger mining business with an operating asset and development expertise. The central question is whether that combination can supply the capital and execution needed to bring Australia's Mt Todd gold project into production. (TSXV:ARTG) operates the Blackwater mine in British Columbia and expects its future cash generation to support Mt Todd. That offers Vista Gold a potential funding source alongside a team experienced in building and operating mines. The financial starting point explains the appeal. Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN:VGZ) ended June 2026 with $49.5 million in cash and no debt. Management described that cash as sufficient for interim development objectives. Joining an operating producer could broaden the resources available for the much larger task of construction. The acquisition requires no cash consideration or new acquisition debt. If Blackwater's expansions perform as planned, the combined business could fund development with less dependence on a separate project-financing package. That could improve the prospects of turning a development asset into an operating mine. Bear Case Mt Todd would sit behind other projects in the spending queue. Blackwater's Phase 1A and EP2 expansions remain the priority, with EP2 completion expected by mid-2028. Mt Todd construction spending is expected after EP2 reaches full production. That sequence makes funding dependent on execution elsewhere. Expansion delays, higher costs, or weaker gold prices could reduce the cash available for Mt Todd. Investors need to distinguish expected future cash generation from money committed to a construction budget. The ownership trade-off also matters. Holders of Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN:VGZ) would exchange their standalone investment for a minority interest in the combined business. Their returns would increasingly depend on the buyer's broader capital-allocation decisions, including how much cash goes to Blackwater, Mt Todd or shareholder distributions. Until those conditions are satisfied, the proposed development route remains contingent on completing the acquisition. These calculations use the announced estimates and span different payment dates. Final adjustments, taxes, and transaction costs will determine how much cash becomes available for deployment. (NYSE:TWI) expects an early-January 2027 closing, subject to regulatory approvals and customary conditions. The expected adjustments can change, and the earnout remains conditional. Acquisitions could also absorb proceeds that investors might otherwise expect to support debt reduction.
