articles.title: May Mobility's SPAC Merger: Is This a Road to Nowhere for Investors?
articles.content: May Mobility's SPAC Merger: Is This a Road to Nowhere for Investors? Daniel Miller, The Motley Fool September 22, 2026 6 min read ACGC NVDA Investors eager to buy into the futuristic vision of profitable driverless vehicles will get their chance soon . May Mobility is aiming to become the first U.S. publicly listed pure-play option for an autonomous ride-hailing technology company. It is poised to go public through a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), merging with ACP Holdings Acquisition (NASDAQ: ACGC) that values the combined company at roughly $1.4 billion. It's expected to operate as May Mobility. trading on the Nasdaq exchange under MAY. But before investors get too excited, let's pump the brakes and take a look at the details. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Opportunity knocks It's easy for investors to get excited about the opportunity, but many might not be aware of the potential market size or growth prospects. The global robotaxi market is projected to reach about $415 billion by 2035, with the U.S. accounting for a roughly $48 billion slice of that pie. The fleet of U.S. commercial autonomous vehicles (AVs) is projected to expand from only about 4,000 vehicles currently to around 35,000 by 2030 -- or about 8% of the ride-sharing market. A year ago this month, Bank of America projected that the long-term U.S. total addressable market (TAM) for AV ride-hailing is a trillion-dollar opportunity as companies such as May Mobility aim to replace the drivers that take roughly 70% of every fare. It's also important for investors to realize how early in the game this is: Alphabet 's Waymo, with an estimated $350 million in annualized revenue, would represent only about 0.5% of U.S. ride-hailing bookings. The opportunity is potentially lucrative, albeit still very early in the game. So, what makes May Mobility intriguing? An asset-light transition May Mobility is moving to an asset-light model. At the company's initial U.S. ride-hailing launch site, it estimates the costs for the safety driver; vehicles (financing, depreciation, insurance, maintenance); site operations (fuel/charging, depot operations, and staff); and remote vehicle supervisors, software maintenance, and field engineers. In this asset-heavy scenario, May Mobility's projections put its annual revenue per vehicle between $130,000 to $150,000, as it keeps all the revenue. But because it also incurs all the costs, it checks in with a negative gross margin per vehicle with a safety driver. Story Continues Under its asset-light model, which includes removing the safety driver, May Mobility transfers the vehicle costs as well as the site operating costs to a fleet operating partner, although it will still incur the costs for remote supervisors, field engineers, and software maintenance. This scenario would come with a larger fleet size thanks to a fleet-operator partner, and lower revenue ($50,000 to $72,000 per vehicle) as it splits the sales with that partner. But it checks in with a gross margin per vehicle between $35,000 to $50,000 annually because it would push off significant costs and could scale up more quickly without needing to purchase and own the fleet. There's further upside with management targeting a 50% reduction in its bill of materials (BOM) by the end of 2028. That's from cost savings realized through computing and sensors with next-generation chip alternatives and as lidar/radar/camera markets scale up and mature. May Mobility also expects to reduce its BOM through cost reductions in hardware components and integration when its software could be installed by the original equipment manufacturer (with Toyota as a partner for AV-ready vehicle platforms at scale) rather than installing it in vehicles afterwards. Over the long term without drivers, management is targeting gross margins of about 70%, and margins under earnings before interest and taxes around 30%. How going public helps When the SPAC deal and merger closes, it could provide May Mobility with up to $337 million in funding. Investors can look at the economics and do the math: In 2025, the company generated roughly $10 million in revenue with a 27% gross margin, while burning $93 million in cash. The SPAC funds should enable it to strengthen its balance sheet and liquidity, finance added research and development, invest in the supply chain to reduce costs, and launch new in markets without drivers. However, without a major cash pile, the cash burn could erode its liquidity rather quickly. What it all means It's an exciting time in an automotive industry that's poised to evolve rapidly over the next decade. However, investors must understand that this is an exceptionally high-risk investment currently. May Mobility's 27% gross margin is an encouraging beginning, but the cash burn is significant and will only increase in the near term. It will rely heavily on the $337 million of fresh capital from its public debut, and that could erode rapidly. Investors also have to consider that despite being in the early innings, there are some heavyweights accelerating forward, including market leader Waymo and Tesla 's slow but steady progress with its Cybercab business. Tesla's Cybercab. Image source: Tesla. May Mobility is intriguing, but this only scratches the surface. Potential shareholders must read through the investor presentation, available here , and recognize that this could end in a total loss. For now, this should be a company that most retail investors watch curiously from the sidelines, especially as this debut tests investor demand for a pure-play AV ride-hailing company. articles.title: SK Hynix Is Eyeing Intel’s (INTC) Ohio Site. Why Micron (MU) Should Pay Attention
articles.content: SK Hynix Is Eyeing Intel’s (INTC) Ohio Site. Why Micron (MU) Should Pay Attention Habib Ur Rehman September 23, 2026 3 min read INTC SKHY MU SK Hynix is exploring something it has never done before: manufacturing memory chips in the United States. Reuters reported on September 16 that the Korean memory giant is discussing several possibilities with Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC ), including leasing part of Intel's long-delayed Ohio complex or forming a venture involving Intel and large cloud customers. SK Hynix said no specific plan has been finalized. For Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU ), the talks matter because one of its strongest strategic advantages is being the major U.S.-based memory producer while AI has made DRAM and HBM increasingly scarce. SK Hynix May Move Into Intel’s $100 Billion Ohio Fab. Micron Has a Reason to Watch SK Hynix Could Give Intel Another Path for Its Delayed Ohio Site Intel has committed enormous capital to Ohio, with the broader project potentially reaching around $100 billion over time. Delays have pushed planned production into the next decade. A tenant or joint-venture partner could therefore help Intel share the financial burden of developing the Ohio site rather than relying entirely on its own foundry demand to justify the buildout. That is the bull case. The bear case is that exploratory talks are a long way from revenue. Bringing advanced Korean memory production to the U.S. could face cost problems, technology-transfer restrictions and objections from Seoul. Intel still needs its core manufacturing roadmap to work. Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) sits on the other side of the equation. AI demand has pushed memory pricing and availability into a strong cycle, and Micron is already pursuing a large U.S. manufacturing expansion. More domestic manufacturing incentives and customer interest in secure supply support that plan. A successful SK Hynix move could eventually erode part of Micron's U.S.-supply differentiation. U.S. cloud companies would gain another potential domestic supplier, while additional long-term memory capacity could eventually loosen the market that currently supports exceptional pricing. Hedge funds loaded up on both chipmakers Insider Monkey tracked 138 hedge funds holding Intel in Q2, up sharply from 112 in Q1. AQR Capital Management held roughly 10.7 million shares after trimming its stake about 7%. Micron's count rose to 184 funds from 154, one of the stronger quarter-over-quarter increases among large semiconductor names. Coatue Management expanded its MU stake dramatically during the quarter. Intel had about 152.2 million shares sold short as of August 31, roughly 3% of public float and 1.7 days to cover. The talks do not rescue Intel's foundry strategy or weaken Micron overnight. They do show what AI scarcity is doing to the supply chain. Memory manufacturing is becoming strategic enough that SK Hynix is considering putting advanced capacity on American soil, and Intel's delayed Ohio project suddenly gives it a potentially valuable asset to negotiate with. articles.title: Pat Gelsinger Just Backed a $100 Million Challenge to Nvidia’s AI Networking Moat. AMD Could Benefit
articles.content: Pat Gelsinger Just Backed a $100 Million Challenge to Nvidia’s AI Networking Moat. AMD Could Benefit Habib Ur Rehman September 23, 2026 3 min read NVDA AMD INTC Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger is backing a startup that thinks AI's next bottleneck is not the accelerator. It is everything waiting for data to arrive. Delos Data announced on September 15 that it raised more than $100 million to develop networking chips and software for increasingly heterogeneous AI data centers. Playground Global, where Gelsinger is a general partner, joined the round. Reuters reported that Delos is designing the network to work across different types of compute hardware rather than assuming every accelerator comes from NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ). That makes Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD ) an important read-through even though AMD is not an investor in Delos. Pat Gelsinger Just Backed a $100 Million Attack on Nvidia’s AI Networking Moat. AMD Could Benefit For illustration purposes only. Photo by Brett Sayles on Pexels Open networking attacks the strongest part of Nvidia's stack Nvidia does not dominate AI simply because its GPUs are fast. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) sells a tightly integrated system of accelerators, networking, interconnects and software. That makes large clusters easier to deploy and gives customers fewer reasons to mix architectures. Delos is betting the market becomes less uniform as inference expands. Its pitch is that a data center should be able to connect whatever mix of accelerators makes economic sense. Gelsinger described idle compute waiting for data as a major waste of both money and energy. If that architecture works, AMD benefits indirectly. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) has been improving Instinct accelerator performance and winning AI deployments, but every friction point involved in mixing AMD hardware with another vendor's ecosystem protects Nvidia. Hardware-agnostic networking could lower that friction. The counterargument is brutal: Nvidia already has scale, mature software and networking products customers know work. A startup with $100 million of financing is attacking an incumbent that spends billions on research and sells the full rack. Delos also has to prove its claimed performance improvements in commercial deployments. Hedge funds increased exposure to both incumbents Insider Monkey tracked 285 hedge funds holding Nvidia in Q2, up from 275 in Q1. Arrowstreet Capital raised its position 10% to roughly 34.7 million shares. AMD's holder count climbed to 164 from 134, while Marshall Wace held approximately 3.9 million shares after increasing its stake modestly. AMD had about 41.7 million shares sold short as of August 31, equal to roughly 2.6% of float and 2.5 days to cover. Story Continues Delos does not have to replace Nvidia networking to matter. It only has to make mixed AI clusters easier to build. Nvidia's moat is strongest when customers buy the entire system together. Anything that makes the pieces more interchangeable gives AMD and every other accelerator challenger a slightly wider door. articles.content: Why AutoZone Stock Rallied Today Joe Tenebruso, The Motley Fool September 22, 2026 2 min read AZO NVDA Shares of AutoZone (NYSE: AZO) rose on Tuesday after the automotive replacement parts and accessories distributor reported stronger-than-expected profits. Image source: Getty Images. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » AutoZone is expanding its store count at a solid clip AutoZone's net sales grew 5.6% year over year to $6.6 billion in its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which ended on Aug. 29. The auto-parts purveyor opened 175 stores during the quarter and a total of 374 over the trailing 12 months. AutoZone ended the period with 8,031 stores, including 6,863 stores in the U.S., 1,001 in Mexico, and 167 in Brazil. Additionally, same-store sales, which measure revenue from locations open for at least a year, increased by 2.7%, or 1.5% when excluding foreign currency fluctuations. "We grew our total store count, opening the most stores ever in a single year, improved on our assortment and in-stock positions, and continued to invest in systems to deliver even better customer service," CEO Phil Daniele said during a conference call with analysts. Better still, tariff refunds helped to drive AutoZone's operating profit up by 10% to $1.3 billion. Its net income, in turn, increased 11% to $931.6 million. And its earnings per share, boosted by stock buybacks, jumped 15% to $56.05. That topped Wall Street's estimates, which had called for per-share profits of $53.89, according to Yahoo! Finance. Management sees further growth in the U.S. and internationally Despite higher gas prices and a challenging overall economic environment, AutoZone expects more gains in the year ahead. "Over the last eight weeks of the quarter, our sales results strengthened, and we feel we are well-positioned for sales growth in fiscal 2027," Daniele said. articles.title: Why Bernstein Still Sees 46% Upside in Zscaler (ZS) but Downgraded Palo Alto (PANW)
articles.content: Why Bernstein Still Sees 46% Upside in Zscaler (ZS) but Downgraded Palo Alto (PANW) Habib Ur Rehman September 23, 2026 3 min read ZS PANW Wall Street has spent much of 2026 rewarding cybersecurity stocks for the risks created by AI. Bernstein now thinks the easy part of that trade is over, with one major exception. Bernstein analyst Peter Weed raised his target on Zscaler, Inc. (NASDAQ: ZS ) to $298 and maintained an Outperform rating on September 17. The target implied roughly 46% upside when the call was published. At the same time, Bernstein downgraded Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (NASDAQ: PANW ) and several other cyber names to Market Perform. The distinction is valuation rather than a belief that AI security demand disappears. Bernstein Says Zscaler Is the Only Cyber Stock With Big Upside Left. Palo Alto Just Got Downgraded Zscaler has to prove its underperformance created an opportunity Zscaler entered the analyst call down about 11.5% in 2026 while many peers had rallied. Bernstein argued that its shift from opportunity-based selling toward deeper customer relationships is beginning to work. Zscaler reported a 115% dollar-based net retention rate in fiscal Q1, and management later said that level had remained fairly stable for several quarters. For Zscaler, Inc. (NASDAQ:ZS), that creates a straightforward rerating case. If existing customers adopt more products while AI increases the number of users, agents and workloads requiring security, growth can remain strong without the stock carrying the same expectations as hotter peers. There is a reason the discount exists. Zscaler still faces slower incremental ARR growth and aggressive competition from companies bundling multiple security functions. If large enterprises prefer consolidation, a focused zero-trust specialist must keep proving it deserves separate budget. Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (NASDAQ:PANW) has almost the opposite problem. Its broad platform gives enterprises a single vendor across network, cloud and security operations, and acquisitions have expanded that reach. Bernstein's downgrade reflects the price investors are already paying for that strength. Integration costs, a larger share count and slowing growth comparisons raise the hurdle. Fund positioning does not show investors abandoning either name Insider Monkey tracked 52 hedge funds holding Zscaler in Q2, up from 46 in Q1. Palo Alto ownership edged up to 89 funds from 87. Fisher Asset Management increased its PANW position 2,143% to about 5.8 million shares. Zscaler's August 31 short-interest snapshot was about 6.35 million shares, roughly 4.7% of public float and 2.9 days to cover. Bernstein's call is interesting because it is not simply bullish cybersecurity commentary. It draws a line inside an already popular trade. Palo Alto may remain the stronger platform business, but Zscaler now has something PANW increasingly lacks: a valuation setup where Wall Street can still imagine a large rerating. articles.title: “The New Clippy”: Benioff Uses Salesforce’s Biggest Product Launch in Years to Challenge Microsoft
articles.content: “The New Clippy”: Benioff Uses Salesforce’s Biggest Product Launch in Years to Challenge Microsoft Sheryar Siddiq September 23, 2026 4 min read CRM MSFT Marc Benioff is never one to pass up a chance to take a jab at Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ), and Dreamforce 2026 was no different. The Salesforce CEO used the company's flagship annual conference in San Francisco to announce AIforce, the biggest product launch Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE: CRM ) has made in years, and to once again refer to Microsoft's Copilot as "the new Clippy," doubling down on a dig he made two years ago. What is Salesforce's (CRM) Economic Moat, and is it Widening or Narrowing? What AIforce Actually Does Salesforce is positioning AIforce as an open, provider-agnostic layer rather than a single proprietary assistant. It's intended to work across multiple AI systems, including Anthropic's Claude, via a specific integration called Claudeforce, which Salesforce claims guarantees zero data retention by the model provider, as well as ChatGPT, Slack, and other environments. Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) made the announcement alongside an additional strategic marker: a fiscal 2030 revenue target of $63 billion, which management reiterated at Dreamforce. A Rivalry That Goes Back To 2024 Benioff portrayed AIforce as the solution to what he calls the "Fantasyland" problem, arguing that competing AI solutions, including Copilot, lack the dependable, controlled business-data layer required to consistently run enterprise operations. It's a continuation of a public feud that's been going on since at least Dreamforce 2024, when Benioff first compared Copilot to Clippy, Microsoft's widely mocked, uninvited desktop assistant from the late 1990s, saying, "We all know now that Microsoft Copilot is basically the new Microsoft Clippy, that customers have not gotten value from it." He's returned to that theme several times since, including at Davos, in an October 2024 written critique saying that Microsoft "lacks the data, metadata, and enterprise security models to create real corporate intelligence," and on a podcast where he labeled Copilot a "tremendous disservice" to the AI sector. Favorable Analyst Response Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) shares closed at $255.65 on September 15, after a nearly 34% rally in the previous month following a rough start to 2026 that saw the stock tumble as much as 37%. That momentum was fueled by Salesforce's most recent quarterly results, which featured $11.35 billion in revenue, exceeding Wall Street's projections on both the top and bottom lines. Analyst reaction to the Dreamforce announcements was also favorable, with Stifel raising its price target for Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) to $300 from $275 while reaffirming a Buy rating, citing six distinct revenue channels laid out by the company for monetizing its new AI stack, including additional core licenses, premium SKU upgrades, Agentforce spending, Data 360, Agent Fabric and Guardian, and APIs, MCPs and related infrastructure. Story Continues Institutional Positioning Institutional posture shifted in similar directions for the two competitors. Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) saw hedge fund ownership fall slightly, from 101 in the first quarter to 99 in the second. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) experienced a greater fall, from 282 funds to 273, though both declines predate the Dreamforce event and are more likely to reflect broader software-sector positioning moves than a direct read on this contest. How AIforce Takes On Copilot Salesforce's pitch for AIforce as an open layer that brings Salesforce data, permissions and business logic into Claude, ChatGPT and other AI interfaces could still be an important competitive distinction, particularly for companies that want to use Salesforce context across multiple AI environments. The emphasis on regulated data access and zero data retention in Claudeforce directly addresses enterprise trust problems, which have hampered AI adoption elsewhere. Conference Hype, Unclear Pricing, and Microsoft's Distribution Juggernaut However, Salesforce's stock has a documented history of rallying on analyst upgrades and conference announcements before reversing those gains, as seen with earlier JPMorgan and Citi buy calls in 2026, and pricing and adoption uncertainty around Agentforce remain unanswered questions even as new products pile on top of it. Microsoft's competition is also far from theoretical, considering Copilot's distribution advantage via Office and Dynamics 365. Insider Monkey's Bottom Line Investors should keep an eye on whether this round of enthusiasm lasts longer than previous Dreamforce-fueled surges, with confirmation likely to come from the next quarterly report, which will show whether Agentforce and now AIforce adoption numbers are translating into the kind of Data and AI revenue growth analysts are projecting with their newly set $300 price targets. Given the remaining uncertainty around how quickly Salesforce can convert AI adoption into meaningful revenue, the more reliable signal for investors will be concrete adoption and revenue-conversion data in upcoming earnings, rather than the announcement itself or the pre-Dreamforce rally that followed Salesforce's latest earnings report. While we acknowledge the potential of CRM as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. articles.title: Nike (NKE): Wall Street Tests Whether the Turnaround Can Outrun Weak Demand Ahead of Q1 Results
articles.content: Nike (NKE): Wall Street Tests Whether the Turnaround Can Outrun Weak Demand Ahead of Q1 Results Faheem Tahir September 23, 2026 5 min read NKE NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) heads into its October 1 fiscal 2027 first-quarter report with Wall Street focused less on whether revenue can beat a modest guide and more on whether improving margins and performance categories can offset weak demand in the lifestyle business. The latest warning comes from Stifel, which cut its price target to $40 from $45 on September 21 while keeping a Hold rating. The firm expects a more promotional Western marketplace and a tougher fiscal fourth-quarter gross-margin comparison, cutting its FY2027 and FY2028 adjusted EPS estimates by $0.20 each, to $1.70 and $2.05. Nike (NKE): Wall Street Tests Whether the Turnaround Can Outrun Weak Demand Ahead of Q1 Results Mbuso Sydwell Nkosi/Shutterstock.com The Bull Case: Sport, Wholesale and the World Cup Can Buy Nike Time There are still tangible signs that NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE)'s reset is working in parts of the portfolio. Performance grew mid-single digits in fiscal 2026, while Running posted five consecutive quarters of double-digit growth and added roughly $1 billion in revenue. North American wholesale revenue grew 10% in the fourth quarter, and management said the business benefited from lower returns, cancellations and discounts rather than simply pushing more inventory into stores. The World Cup provides another near-term tailwind. Stifel estimates the tournament could add about $300 million to Q1 revenue, while NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) has already pointed to stronger football demand and said its World Cup product launches were gaining traction. Stifel also continues to expect revenue above consensus, noting that Nike has exceeded its own revenue guidance for seven consecutive quarters. Margin improvement could provide another offset. NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE)'s Q4 gross margin, excluding the $986 million tariff-recovery benefit, was down just 10 basis points year-over-year, better than its guidance. Management attributed the improvement partly to lower discounts, cancellations and sales-related reserves and expects supply-chain restructuring to support margins in FY2027. The Bear Case: The New Product Pipeline Still Has to Prove Itself The problem is that NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE)'s strongest performance categories are not yet large enough to erase weakness elsewhere. Sportswear declined double digits in Q4, while management expects Sportswear and Jordan streetwear to remain negative through FY2027, even with improvement in the second half. Together, those businesses represent roughly half of revenue. That is where Stifel's latest update becomes important. The firm sees insufficient consumer demand for Nike's new products and continued contraction in Hoops Classics, which represents about 18% of revenue. UBS has also pointed to deteriorating global sales trends and expects a Q1 EPS miss, while Citi sees elevated promotions and difficult North American comparisons weighing on Q2. Baird similarly cited weaker marketplace conditions, more negative retailer commentary on athletic lifestyle sales and pressure from Nike's China e-commerce reset. Story Continues China remains another unresolved drag. Greater China revenue fell 17% in Q4, and management expects near-term trends to remain broadly consistent with that decline. Although full-price realization and sell-through have improved in some areas, NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) is still cleaning up inventory and reducing supply into the market. Valuation Premium Faces Growing Skepticism Nike's valuation and positioning add another layer to that debate. The stock traded at a 20.66 forward P/E as of September 21, compared with 10.46 for Deckers Outdoor, 14.27 for On Holding and 11.47 for Adidas. Hedge fund ownership also fell to 56 funds in the second quarter from 71 in the first, although several individual managers increased their stakes sharply. Arrowstreet Capital raised its position 10,175% to 5.62 million shares, while Renaissance Technologies increased its stake 1,192% to 4.07 million shares. Meanwhile, short interest climbed to 75.59 million shares as of August 31 from 57.37 million a month earlier, putting short interest at 7.92% of the float and 5.10% of shares outstanding. The combination leaves NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) with a higher valuation than several peers alongside reduced hedge fund participation and rising short interest, making evidence of a broader recovery increasingly important. The Takeaway: Q1 Is About the Quality of the Recovery The October 1 report therefore faces a higher bar than the headline revenue number suggests. A World Cup boost can support sales, but Wall Street is looking for evidence that demand is broadening beyond Running and football, particularly in Sportswear and Jordan, while gross-margin improvement survives a more promotional marketplace. That tension explains the recent estimate cuts despite some analysts retaining relatively constructive revenue expectations. UBS expects a Q1 EPS shortfall (five cents) and sees risk of a broader FY2027 reset at the November Investor Day, while BMO expects NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) to reset its FY2027 outlook when it reports. For NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE), the key question heading into October 1 is whether the turnaround is beginning to create healthier full-price demand, or merely shifting the mix toward the parts of the portfolio that are already working. The answer will also shape expectations heading into the November 16-17 Investor Day, where management is scheduled to outline the next phase of its growth strategy. While we acknowledge the potential of NKE as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. articles.title: An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich
articles.content: An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on x (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on facebook (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on linkedin (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on whatsapp (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on x (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on facebook (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on linkedin (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Jessica Salter . Photography by Joël Hunn Published September 30 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I moved to Zürich from Geneva when I was four, but I was born in Munich. (My mother is Dutch and my father is German.) I moved back to Germany in my early teens, but I returned here to study economics at the University of St Gallen before completing another degree in economics and philosophy at Harvard. Now I split my time between London and Zürich, working in finance and investments along with writing and performing poetry. I feel very Swiss. Our first home was an apartment near Lake Zürich. But the home I really remember was further out in Schindellegi, a village that feels quite rural despite only being half an hour from the city centre. My childhood memories are mainly sensory: the mountains, the lake. Sound behaves very differently here than in most cities. You feel cocooned. The lake is central to life in Zürich ; when it’s warm, everyone gathers on the water’s edge at weekends and after work. I like sitting on the terrace at Alex Lake Zürich, a hotel right on the water (there’s a little boat that runs back and forth to Storchen, a hotel and restaurant in the city centre). On the northern shore, La Muña has a small rooftop terrace that’s perfect at sunset, with the whole city laid out below. A view of the Limmat river towards Lake Zürich © Joël Hunn Marktgasse in the city centre © Joël Hunn Having a treat there © Joël Hunn Everyone here is sporty and nearly everyone is a semi-professional cyclist. I’m not – I ride a Dutch bike with upright handlebars – and I prefer hiking to cycling. Üetliberg, a mountain just above the city, is the easiest hike; you can walk for a couple of hours. Etzel on the south side of Lake Zürich is a proper half-day walk and there’s a restaurant at the top. For a serious hike, I go to Grosser Mythen , a mountain with steep, hairpin turns. I have been going to Seebad Utoquai, the public baths on the promenade between Bellevue and Zürichhorn, since childhood. You can bathe in the lake too: people even swim to work with all their things in a waterproof bag. I’ve recently joined a group of female entrepreneurs who meet further down the lake towards Richterswil . We do a cold plunge in the lake, then help each other with business plans, funding and networking. On Römergrasse in the city centre © Joël Hunn At Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books © Joël Hunn L’Alsace Heureuse by Hansi on display there © Joël Hunn People think Zürich is very straight-laced, and on the surface it is. But behind closed doors, it’s radically creative. There’s a thriving techno scene: Adriatique and Jenny Cara are based here. In my early 20s, I had a DJ friend who would take me to Kreis 5, which is a bit like London’s Shoreditch. Basel and Zürich are notorious for hating each other because of football, but people come here from Basel for the music; they respect each other’s techno scenes. One of the most beautiful buildings here is the Schweizerische Nationalbank, right in the centre on Börsenstrasse. There is a building next door, the SNB Forum, where you can see bank notes and explore the history of SNB on an interactive LED screen. It also hosts the Karl Brunner Distinguished Lecture Series; I’ve heard American economist John H Cochrane speak there. Growing up in Zürich has been influential in teaching me how a European capital of finance conducts itself. There’s a big focus on family-owned businesses here, so naturally they think about how to exist for many generations. In New York or London, where I’ve also lived and worked, the pace is more rapid, which can feel quite short-term. At the shop of Swiss label Lamarel © Joël Hunn I’ve always spent more money on books than clothes. Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books in the heart of the old town is my favourite bookshop. It specialises in beautiful and rare books from the 15th to 21st centuries – I once found an early edition of one of Else Lasker-Schüler’s poetry collections – and the shop is a centre for literary minds and creatives. Zürich also has brilliant vintage furniture shops, such as Kioskio , which sources pieces from private collections across Europe; the prices are genuinely good. For clothes, I like Lamarel, a Swiss label built around simple, easy shapes. The city has different dress codes depending where you are: around the art schools and design studios in Kreis 4 and Kreis 5, the style is loose and vintage. In the centre it is more conservative, with muted tones and immaculate tailoring. Outside at Trattoria Neumarkt © Joël Hunn Eating a number of dishes there © Joël Hunn Green olives, stracciatella di burrata with chilli crunch and chive, and sourdough bread with miso butter © Joël Hunn The food scene has changed a great deal since I was a child. There used to be only a handful of restaurants serving international cuisine; now there are many. Amia is a new outdoor bar with a French Mediterranean-inspired menu, and I love the confit of char at Bürgli. Trattoria Neumarkt does rotating pop-up menus, often with a Japanese-Italian blend; I go for its Japanese take on cacio e pepe with udon noodles. My Italian partner was initially sceptical but has since been won over. When I want to write, I go to B2 Boutique Hotel, a former brewery near the Google offices that now has the most extraordinary library bar: books floor to ceiling, all the way round. I’ll sit there for hours with a coffee and write. But mostly I find myself going back to the lake. I go down to Bürkliplatz, a town square where you can sit right on the water. I find it endlessly inspiring. Zürich has taught me a sensitivity for atmosphere, silence and order. There’s a layer to the city that makes you attentive to what is not said, and that’s where poetry can happen. BARS, CAF´ÉS & RESTAURANTS Amia restaurantamia.ch Bürgli restaurantbuergli.ch La Muña lareserve-zurich.com Storchen Zürich storchen.ch Trattoria Neumarkt neumarkt-zuerich.ch SHOPPING Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books finebooks.ch Kioskio kioskio.ch Lamarel shoplamarel.com THINGS TO DO Schweizerische Nationalbank snb.ch Seebad Utoquai Utoquai 50, 8008 WHERE TO STAY Alex Lake Zürich alexlakezurich.com B2 Boutique Hotel b2hotel.ch Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Follow the topics in this article Travel Switzerland Zurich How To Spend It In...
